# Synthesized Recommendation: Fuzzy Temporal Retrieval Tool

## 1. Library choice — `dateparser` wins, with a caveat

`dateparser` is actively maintained (2025 releases, Workable fork), handles the long tail Tom listed natively: "last month", "Q1 2024" (with locales), "around March", relative-to-now, plus 200+ locales. It's the canonical Python answer. The 8x perf penalty vs `dateutil` is irrelevant — you're parsing ~2 inputs per tool call, not 10k rows. ([dateparser PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/dateparser/))

`dateutil.parser` with `fuzzy=True` is faster but doesn't grok "Q1" or "last month" without you writing the relative-math yourself. ([dateutil docs](https://dateutil.readthedocs.io/en/stable/parser.html))

`Duckling`/`Heideltime`/`SUTime` are JVM-heavy and overkill — production teams ([Dexlock survey](https://dexlock.com/blog/a-dive-into-nlp-date-parsers/)) only reach for them when probabilistic multi-result extraction matters (chatbots, ambiguous spans). You have one input, you want one range.

**Stack:** `dateparser.parse()` for points, plus a thin shim for "between X and Y" / "before X" / "Q1 2024" that calls `dateparser` twice and emits a `(start, end)` tuple. Use `dateparser.search.search_dates()` only when extracting from node text (see §2).

## 2. Extraction strategy — pre-index, don't scan

The temporal-RAG literature is unanimous: **pre-extract and normalize timestamps at write time** ([Towards Data Science temporal layer](https://towardsdatascience.com/rag-is-blind-to-time-i-built-a-temporal-layer-to-fix-it-in-production/), [arxiv 2510.13590 RAG-Temporal-Graphs](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.13590v1)). Query-time NL-extraction on 4000 nodes is workable today (~2s with `dateparser.search`) but compounds: every recall pays the cost, and you can't index it. Vector DBs all chose the same answer: Weaviate filters `created_at > 2025-01-01` natively, Qdrant has decay functions, Pinecone has metadata filters ([ML Journey comparison](https://mljourney.com/pinecone-vs-weaviate-vs-qdrant-choosing-a-vector-database-for-production-rag/)) — none of them re-parse text on every query.

**Concrete:** add a `node_event_times` table (`node_id`, `event_time`, `confidence`, `extraction_source`) populated by a one-shot backfill (`scripts/extract_event_times.py`) + a hook in `revise()`/`remember()` that runs `dateparser.search` on title+content+kv when text changes. Index `event_time`. Query path stays pure SQL.

## 3. Bi-temporal contract — three named anchors, not booleans

SQL:2011 + Datomic converged on the same three-axis model: **valid time** (when it was true), **transaction time** (when DB learned it), and **decision time** (Datomic adds nothing here; Datomic is unitemporal — XTDB is the bitemporal one). ([Wikipedia temporal db](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temporal_database), [Datomic history docs](https://docs.datomic.com/client-tutorial/history.html), [XTDB bitemp](https://xtdb.com/blog/building-a-bitemp-index-2-resolution))

For your three anchors:
- `event_time` → valid time (the new indexed column)
- `created_at` → transaction time (encoding)
- `updated_at` → last-revision marker (Datomic-style "since")

**API:** one `time_anchor` enum parameter: `"event" | "created" | "updated"`. Default `"event"` (matches user intuition: "what was true at T"). This mirrors Datomic's `:as-of` / `:since` keyword shape — single argument names the axis. ([Datomic Clojure API](https://docs.datomic.com/clojure/index.html))
